Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 50
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Plumber
  trauma_type: Assault
  pcl5: 73

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Threat: Safe Zone Only: I only feel safe in a very limited number of places, Startle to Movement: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger, Sleep Problems: Trouble falling or staying asleep
  Memory: Guilt on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense guilt, Visual Memories: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images., Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.
  Negative Appraisals: No Longer Capable: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me, Injustice: What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it, Self-Doubt: I can't trust that I will do the right thing

Vignette:
Emeka had always been proud of his work as a plumber. For over twenty years, he had built a solid reputation in his community, known for his skill and reliability. His hands, rough and calloused from years of labor, were a testament to his dedication. He was a family man, married to his high school sweetheart, and they had raised two children together. Life was predictable, and Emeka found comfort in the routine of his days. But everything changed one fateful evening when he was attacked on his way home from a job.

The memory of the assault was like a film stuck on replay in his mind, an endless loop of chaos and pain that he could not escape. He had been walking to his car, tools in hand, when he was approached by a group of men. A sudden rush of adrenaline had surged through him as he sensed their hostile intent. The feeling of vulnerability was overwhelming, and despite his attempts to defend himself, he was outnumbered. The blows came quickly, and amid the chaos, he remembered the fearful faces of his children flashing in his mind, their innocence a stark contrast to the brutality of that moment. Since that night, Emeka had struggled with the simplest of tasks. 

His life began to shrink, the places he felt safe dwindling to a few select corners of his home. The living room carried a semblance of normalcy, where he would sit with his family, but even there, the shadows of anxiety loomed large. He found himself jumping at every unexpected sound—the rustle of leaves outside or a sudden movement from his children made his heart race, sending him spiraling back to that night. He had come to believe that the world outside his safe zone was fraught with danger, and the thought of stepping out into it filled him with dread. He told himself it was better to stay home, to avoid the risk of facing that fear head-on.

Sleep, once a welcome respite, had become elusive. Emeka would lie in bed, staring at the ceiling, replaying the attack in vivid detail. The images were sharp in his mind; he could see the faces of his attackers, the glint of a knife, and the sound of his own heart pounding in his ears. But when it came to articulating the experience, words failed him. He felt trapped in a prison of his own making, unable to express the horror that had unfolded. The guilt that accompanied his memories was suffocating. He often thought he should have done something differently, that somehow, he could have prevented the assault. This guilt gnawed at him, making him feel as if he had failed not just himself but also his family, who depended on him.

In the weeks and months following the assault, Emeka found himself withdrawing from the people who mattered most. He avoided social gatherings, fearing that he would be confronted by the unfamiliarity of large crowds or, worse, the possibility of encountering someone from that night. His wife, Amina, noticed the change in him. She often tried to coax him out of his shell, suggesting family outings or gatherings with friends, but he would make excuses, convincing her that he was simply too tired or had too much work to do. The distance between them grew, and he became increasingly aware of the strain he was placing on their marriage.

Emeka’s self-image had taken a significant hit. He felt he was no longer the man he once was, the provider and protector his family relied upon. Thoughts of inadequacy plagued him, and he began to doubt his ability to make even the simplest decisions. This self-doubt only reinforced his desire to retreat further into himself, a cycle that felt unbreakable. 

It was a particularly difficult night when Amina sat beside him, her eyes searching his for answers. She asked him gently if he would consider talking to someone. Emeka felt a flicker of hope and fear intertwine within him. What frightened him most was the vulnerability of opening up about his pain, yet part of him longed to find a way to reclaim the man he used to be. He had come to understand that his silence was hurting not just him but his family as well. It was this realization, amid the turmoil of emotions, that finally motivated him to seek help. Emeka was ready to confront his past, hoping to find a path back to himself and mend the bonds that had begun to fray.
